---
title: "Shiny for Python"
---

This chapter introduces Shiny for Python using the **Core** API. We'll cover the `App`, `ui`, `server`, and `render` components to build the example application we'll use throughout the rest of the book.


## Create app directory

We'll create and move into a new directory (`pyap`, for Python app-package),

```bash
mkdir pyap
cd pyap
```

## Virtual environments

In Python, it's a good idea to use a virtual environment. This practice might be new to R developers, so I'll give a quick overview.[^venv-renv]

[^venv-renv]: Python environments are a similar concept to the [`renv` package in R](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html).

### How virtual environments work

Python virtual environments isolate a project's dependencies, so any packages installed for one project don't conflict with other projects. Two common tools used in this approach are illustrated below:

```{=html}
<style>

  font-family: monospace;
  font-size: 1.5em;
  font-weight: bold;
  color: #9753b8 !important;
  background-color: #f6f6f6;
  padding: 0.2em;
}
</style>
```

```{mermaid}

```

Python's built-in virtual environment tool (`venv`) ships with Python. The general workflow is: 

1. _Create virtual environment (`python -m venv`)_  
2. _Use the environment (`activate`)_   
3. _Install dependencies (`pip install`)_ 

`venv` doesn't have a built-in lockfile, which also means we'll need to also run `pip freeze` to store the dependencies in `requirements.txt`.

`uv` is similar, but has a few more benefits:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: 'uv virtual environments'
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"14px"}}}%%

flowchart TB
    SystemPython[("System Python<br/><code>/usr/bin/python3</code>")]
    
    subgraph UvFlow["uv (Rust-based, fast)"]
        direction TB
        UvCmd["<code>uv venv</code>"]
        UvDir[".venv/<br/>├── bin/python<br/>└── lib/site-packages/"]
        UvAdd["<code>uv add shiny</code>"]
        UvCache[("Global cache<br/><code>~/.cache/uv/</code>")]
        UvLock["<code>uv.lock</code><br/>(reproducible)"]
        
        UvCmd --> UvDir
        UvAdd --> UvCache
        UvCache -->|"hardlink<br/>(near-instant)"| UvDir
        UvAdd --> UvLock
    end
    
    ProjectB["Project B<br/>needs shiny 1.6.1"]
    
    SystemPython --> UvCmd
    
    UvDir -.->|"isolates"| ProjectB

    style UvDir text-align:left
    
    classDef system fill:#2d3748,stroke:#48bb78,color:#fff
    classDef uvStyle fill:#744210,stroke:#f6ad55,color:#fff
    classDef project fill:#553c9a,stroke:#b794f4,color:#fff
    
    class SystemPython system
    class UvCmd,UvDir,UvAdd,UvCache,UvLock uvStyle
    class ProjectB project

```

`uv` requires a separate install command, [^uv-install] but also includes a global cache with hardlinks. During installation, `uv` reuses downloaded dependencies across projects, which is typically faster than copying/downloading them each time (as `venv` does). `uv add` also installs new dependencies in one step, and the `uv.lock` file automatically tracks exact versions. 

Both tools create a `.venv/` folder with an isolated Python interpreter and its own `site-packages/` directory. When activated, the shell points to *that* Python instead of the **System Python.** So, `pip install shiny` only installs `shiny` in *this* project. 

[^uv-install]: Install `uv` from the Terminal with: `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`

### Virtual environment setup

Install `uv` with:

**macOS/Linux**:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

After installation, restart your terminal (or run `source ~/.local/bin/env` on macOS/Linux) so the `uv` binary is on your `PATH`.

**Windows (PowerShell)**

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Create a virtual environment, defaults to `.venv`:

```bash
uv venv
```

If you don't want to install/use `uv`, you can use Python's built-in `venv`:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the virtual environment:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

The terminal prompt will prepend with `(pyap)`.

**Windows (PowerShell)**:

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 
```

### Installing dependencies in virtual environments

Now we can install Shiny into the `venv`:

```bash
uv pip install shiny
```

## Hello Shiny

The first app in this chapter is the Old Faithful histogram we saw at the start of the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter. In the Whole Game, we moved this app into a package without looking closely at how it works. Here we'll slow down and walk through each piece of the Core API.

If you're following along with the [`pyap`](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/pyap) repository, check out the `02.1_shiny-app` branch:

```bash
git checkout 02.1_shiny-app
```

The branch contains a single `app.py` file (along with a `README.md` and a `.gitignore`). The app imports `matplotlib` and `numpy` in addition to `shiny`, so we'll install both into the virtual environment before running it:

```bash
uv pip install matplotlib numpy
```

The `.venv/` folder isn't tracked by Git, so the same virtual environment stays in place when we switch branches. Each time we check out a new branch, we install whatever new packages that branch needs (the chapter will point these out).

### app.py

The full contents of `app.py` are below:

```python
# This is a Shiny for Python application.
# Run it with: shiny run app.py

from shiny import App, ui, render
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Old Faithful geyser waiting time data (bimodal distribution)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
waiting = np.concatenate([
    rng.normal(54, 5, 100),   # short-wait eruption cluster
    rng.normal(80, 6, 172),   # long-wait eruption cluster
])

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_slider(
            "bins",
            "Number of bins:",
            min=1,
            max=50,
            value=30,
        ),
    ),
    ui.output_plot("distPlot"),
    title="Old Faithful Geyser Data",
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render.plot
    def distPlot():
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.hist(waiting, bins=input.bins(), color="darkgray", edgecolor="white")
        ax.set_xlabel("Waiting time to next eruption (in mins)")
        ax.set_title("Histogram of waiting times")
        return fig


app = App(app_ui, server)
```

Every Core API app is built from the same three parts: a UI object, a server function, and a call to `App()` that combines them. The `waiting` data are created at the top of the file (outside the server), so they're computed once when the app starts rather than each time the plot is drawn.

### Imports

The first line imports the three Core API components we'll use from `shiny`:

```python
from shiny import App, ui, render
```

`ui` holds the functions for building the layout, inputs, and outputs. `render` holds the decorators that turn Python functions into outputs, and `App` is the class that builds the application object.

### UI

The UI is a nested set of function calls stored in `app_ui`. `ui.page_sidebar()` creates a page with a sidebar on the left and a main content area on the right:

```python
app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_slider(
            "bins",
            "Number of bins:",
            min=1,
            max=50,
            value=30,
        ),
    ),
    ui.output_plot("distPlot"),
    title="Old Faithful Geyser Data",
)
```

The first argument to `ui.page_sidebar()` is the `ui.sidebar()`, and everything after it goes in the main area. The sidebar holds a single slider input, `ui.input_slider()`, which takes an id (`"bins"`), a label, and the `min`, `max`, and starting `value`. The main area holds `ui.output_plot()`, which reserves space for a plot with the id `"distPlot"`.

These two ids are how the UI and server find each other. The server reads the slider value using `"bins"`, and it sends the plot back to the space reserved by `"distPlot"`.

### Server

The server is a function that Shiny calls once for each user session. It takes three arguments: `input`, `output`, and `session`:

```python
def server(input, output, session):
    @render.plot
    def distPlot():
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.hist(waiting, bins=input.bins(), color="darkgray", edgecolor="white")
        ax.set_xlabel("Waiting time to next eruption (in mins)")
        ax.set_title("Histogram of waiting times")
        return fig
```

Outputs are defined as functions inside the server. The `@render.plot` line is a [decorator](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-decorator), a function that wraps the function defined below it. In this case, it tells Shiny that `distPlot()` returns a plot. The function name is the output id, so `distPlot()` fills the space created by `ui.output_plot("distPlot")` in the UI.[^shiny-render]

[^shiny-render]: The decorated function replaces the `output$distPlot <- renderPlot({...})` assignment we'd write in R.

Inside `distPlot()`, the slider value is read with `input.bins()`. Inputs are reactive values, so we call them like functions to get their current value.[^shiny-input] Reading `input.bins()` inside a render function also creates a reactive dependency: whenever the slider moves, Shiny re-runs `distPlot()` and redraws the histogram. The function builds the histogram with `matplotlib` and returns the figure, which `@render.plot` displays in the app.

[^shiny-input]: `input.bins()` is the Python equivalent of `input$bins`. The parentheses are easy to forget, especially if you're used to R.

We don't use `output` or `session` in this app, but we'll see them again when we cover modules and reactive patterns in later chapters.

### App

The last line combines the UI and server into a Shiny application:[^shiny-app]

```python
app = App(app_ui, server)
```

[^shiny-app]: `App()` plays the same role as `shinyApp()` in R.

The name of this object matters. When we run the app, Shiny looks for an object named `app` in `app.py` by default.

### Run the app

With the virtual environment activated, we can launch the app from the terminal with `shiny run`:

```bash
shiny run app.py
```

Shiny starts a local web server and prints its address in the terminal (`http://127.0.0.1:8000` by default). Open the address in a browser to view the app, and move the slider to confirm the histogram updates with the number of bins.

During development, the same `--reload` and `--launch-browser` flags we used in the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter restart the app whenever we save a change and open it in a browser automatically:

```bash
shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py
```

Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> in the terminal to stop the app.

## Movies app

The Old Faithful app is a good introduction, but it's too small to show the problems that come up as an app grows. The app we'll use for the rest of the book is a scatter plot of movie review data, and it has more inputs, a helper function in a separate file, and a dataset that's read from disk. The code and data come from the [Building Web Applications with Shiny](https://rstudio-education.github.io/shiny-course/) course.

Check out the `02.2_movies-app` branch to follow along:

```bash
git checkout 02.2_movies-app
```

The branch replaces the Old Faithful code with three files:

```default
pyap/
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
└── utils.py
```

The movies app reads the data with `pandas`, so we'll install it into the virtual environment (`shiny` and `matplotlib` are already installed):

```bash
uv pip install pandas
```

::: {.callout-note title="pandas or polars?" collapse="true"}

This book uses `pandas` because it's more common in Shiny for Python examples (roughly 3 to 1 over [`polars`](https://pola.rs/) in the [`py-shiny`](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny) and [`py-shiny-templates`](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny-templates) repositories as of 2026-10). Shiny doesn't force the choice, though: `@render.data_frame` accepts both `pandas` and `polars` DataFrames. To follow along with `polars` instead, install it into the virtual environment:

```bash
uv pip install polars
```

`polars` builds queries from column expressions (like `pl.col("genre")`), so its syntax will feel familiar if you're coming from `dplyr`.

:::

### app.py

The full `app.py` for the movies app is below:

```python
# Run with: shiny run app.py
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import pandas as pd
from utils import scatter_plot

movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_select(
            "y",
            "Y-axis:",
            choices={
                "imdb_rating": "IMDB rating",
                "imdb_num_votes": "IMDB number of votes",
                "critics_score": "Critics Score",
                "audience_score": "Audience Score",
                "runtime": "Runtime",
            },
            selected="audience_score",
        ),
        ui.input_select(
            "x",
            "X-axis:",
            choices={
                "imdb_rating": "IMDB rating",
                "imdb_num_votes": "IMDB number of votes",
                "critics_score": "Critics Score",
                "audience_score": "Audience Score",
                "runtime": "Runtime",
            },
            selected="critics_score",
        ),
        ui.input_select(
            "z",
            "Color by:",
            choices={
                "title_type": "Title Type",
                "genre": "Genre",
                "mpaa_rating": "MPAA Rating",
                "critics_rating": "Critics Rating",
                "audience_rating": "Audience Rating",
            },
            selected="mpaa_rating",
        ),
        ui.input_slider(
            "alpha", "Alpha:", min=0.0, max=1.0, value=0.4, step=0.05
        ),
        ui.input_slider("size", "Size:", min=1, max=5, value=3),
        ui.input_text(
            "plot_title",
            "Plot title",
            placeholder="Enter text to be used as plot title",
        ),
        ui.input_action_button("update_plot_title", "Update plot title"),
    ),
    ui.p(
        "These data were obtained from ",
        ui.a("IMDB", href="http://www.imdb.com/"),
        " and ",
        ui.a("Rotten Tomatoes", href="https://www.rottentomatoes.com/"),
        ".",
    ),
    ui.p(
        f"The data represent {len(movies)} randomly sampled movies "
        "released between 1972 to 2014 in the United States."
    ),
    ui.output_plot("scatterplot"),
    ui.hr(),
    ui.p(
        ui.em(
            "The code for this Shiny application comes from ",
            ui.a(
                "Building Web Applications with Shiny",
                href="https://rstudio-education.github.io/shiny-course/",
            ),
        )
    ),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    # only updates title when button is clicked, runs on init with empty string
    @reactive.calc
    @reactive.event(input.update_plot_title, ignore_none=False, ignore_init=False)
    def new_plot_title():
        return input.plot_title().title()

    @render.plot
    def scatterplot():
        return scatter_plot(
            df=movies,
            x_var=input.x(),
            y_var=input.y(),
            col_var=input.z(),
            alpha_var=input.alpha(),
            size_var=input.size(),
            title=new_plot_title(),
        )


app = App(app_ui, server)
```

The structure is the same as the Old Faithful app: imports, a UI object, a server function, and `App()`. The differences are in what each part contains, so we'll focus on those below.

### Reading data

The app reads `movies.csv` into a `pandas` [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html) (a table of rows and named columns) at the top of the file:

```python
movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
```

Like `waiting` in the Old Faithful app, `movies` is created outside the server, so the file is read once when the app starts and every session shares the same data. The path is relative, which means Python looks for `movies.csv` in the current working directory. We need to run the app from the folder that holds `movies.csv` (we'll fix this fragile path when we store the data inside the package in the [Data](data.qmd) chapter).

The data have 34 columns describing each movie (`title`, `genre`, `runtime`, `mpaa_rating`, `imdb_rating`, `critics_score`, `audience_score`, and others). The app only plots a handful of them.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading data with polars" collapse="true"}

The code blocks below import the package, read `movies.csv`, and count rows in `pandas`, `polars`, and the tidyverse:

`pandas`:

```python
import pandas as pd

movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
len(movies)
```

`polars`:

```python
import polars as pl

movies = pl.read_csv("movies.csv", null_values="NA")
len(movies)
```

R (tidyverse):

```r
library(readr)

movies <- read_csv("movies.csv")
nrow(movies)
```

`pandas` reads the string `NA` as a missing value by default, but `polars` only treats empty fields as missing. Because `movies.csv` stores missing values as `NA`, `pl.read_csv("movies.csv")` fails with a parsing error, so we pass the string to `null_values`.

:::

### Inputs

The sidebar holds seven inputs. Three of them are `ui.input_select()` dropdowns for the x axis, the y axis, and the color variable. Each dropdown takes a `choices` dictionary, where the keys are the values sent to the server and the values are the labels displayed in the app:[^shiny-choices]

```python
ui.input_select(
    "y",
    "Y-axis:",
    choices={
        "imdb_rating": "IMDB rating",
        "imdb_num_votes": "IMDB number of votes",
        "critics_score": "Critics Score",
        "audience_score": "Audience Score",
        "runtime": "Runtime",
    },
    selected="audience_score",
),
```

[^shiny-choices]: This is the reverse of a named vector in R's `selectInput()`, where the names are the labels (`c("IMDB rating" = "imdb_rating")`).

When a user picks "Critics Score" from the dropdown, `input.y()` returns `"critics_score"`, which is the column name we need for the plot. `selected` sets the starting value.

The two `ui.input_slider()` calls control the transparency (`alpha`) and size of the points. The `alpha` slider uses `step=0.05` to move in small increments between `0.0` and `1.0`.

The last two inputs work together. `ui.input_text()` creates a text box for the plot title, and `ui.input_action_button()` creates a button that applies it. We'll see how the server connects them below.

### UI text

The main area holds more than the plot output. `ui.p()`, `ui.a()`, `ui.em()`, and `ui.hr()` create HTML paragraph, link, emphasis, and horizontal rule tags. Positional arguments become the tag's contents, and keyword arguments (like `href`) become its attributes:

```python
ui.p(
    "These data were obtained from ",
    ui.a("IMDB", href="http://www.imdb.com/"),
    " and ",
    ui.a("Rotten Tomatoes", href="https://www.rottentomatoes.com/"),
    ".",
),
```

The second paragraph uses an [f-string](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html#formatted-string-literals) to insert the number of rows in `movies` with `len(movies)`. Because the UI is built once when the app starts, this number is computed once too (it isn't reactive).

### Reactive outputs

The server has two functions. `scatterplot()` is the output, and it follows the same pattern as `distPlot()` in the Old Faithful app: the `@render.plot` decorator, a function name that matches the `ui.output_plot("scatterplot")` id, and calls to `input.x()`, `input.y()`, and the other inputs. Each input read inside `scatterplot()` is a reactive dependency, so changing any dropdown or slider redraws the plot.

The plot title works differently. We don't want the title to change with every keystroke in the text box, only when the button is clicked. `new_plot_title()` handles this with two decorators from the `reactive` module:

```python
@reactive.calc
@reactive.event(input.update_plot_title, ignore_none=False, ignore_init=False)
def new_plot_title():
    return input.plot_title().title()
```

Decorators are applied from the bottom up, so we'll read them in that order:

1. `@reactive.event()` limits when the function runs. It only responds to `input.update_plot_title` (the button), and it ignores changes to `input.plot_title()` even though the function reads it.
2. `ignore_none=False` and `ignore_init=False` let the function run once when the app starts (before the button has been clicked), so the first plot is drawn with an empty title instead of waiting for a click.
3. `@reactive.calc` turns the function into a reactive calculation, which caches its result and returns it to any output that calls `new_plot_title()`.[^shiny-event]

[^shiny-event]: Together, these decorators do the same job as `eventReactive(input$update_plot_title, ..., ignoreNULL = FALSE)` in R.

`.title()` is a Python string method that capitalizes the first letter of each word, so typing `critics vs audience` and clicking the button gives the plot the title "Critics Vs Audience". `scatterplot()` calls `new_plot_title()` just like an input, which makes the reactive calculation one of its dependencies.

### Utility functions

`app.py` doesn't build the plot itself. The plotting code lives in `scatter_plot()`, a function in `utils.py`:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd


def scatter_plot(df, x_var, y_var, col_var, alpha_var, size_var, title=""):
    """Create a scatter plot of df colored by a categorical variable."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    categories = sorted(df[col_var].dropna().unique())
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
    for i, cat in enumerate(categories):
        subset = df[df[col_var] == cat]
        ax.scatter(
            subset[x_var],
            subset[y_var],
            alpha=alpha_var,
            s=size_var ** 2 * 10,
            color=cmap(i % 10),
            label=str(cat),
        )
    ax.set_xlabel(x_var.replace("_", " ").title())
    ax.set_ylabel(y_var.replace("_", " ").title())
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(
        title=col_var.replace("_", " ").title(),
        bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1),
        loc="upper left",
    )
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig
```

`matplotlib` doesn't map a categorical variable to colors automatically, so `scatter_plot()` loops over each category in `col_var` and draws its points with a color from the `tab10` palette. The `s` argument sets the marker area, so `size_var ** 2 * 10` scales the slider's 1 to 5 range into visible point sizes. The axis and legend labels are built from the column names (`critics_score` becomes "Critics Score"), and the legend is placed outside the plot area so it doesn't cover any points.

::: {.callout-note title="Filtering with polars" collapse="true"}

The code blocks below show the two `pandas` operations in `scatter_plot()` next to their `polars` and `dplyr` equivalents (selecting the rows in a category, and the unique values with no missing entries):

`pandas`:

```python
df[df[col_var] == cat]
df[col_var].dropna().unique()
```

`polars`:

```python
df.filter(pl.col(col_var) == cat)
df[col_var].drop_nulls().unique()
```

R (dplyr):

```r
filter(df, .data[[col_var]] == cat)
unique(na.omit(df[[col_var]]))
```

`pl.col(col_var)` refers to a column by name inside an expression, much like `.data[[col_var]]` in `dplyr`. Using it requires `import polars as pl` at the top of `utils.py`. `polars` doesn't preserve the order of `unique()` results by default, but `scatter_plot()` already wraps them in `sorted()`.

:::

Moving this code out of `app.py` keeps the server short, and it gives us a plain Python function we can call (and test) without running the app. `app.py` imports it with `from utils import scatter_plot`, which works because `utils.py` sits in the same folder as `app.py`. This is the same idea behind the `geyser_waiting()` function we added in the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter, and it's where the package structure in later chapters starts to pay off.

### Run the movies app

We launch the movies app the same way we launched the Old Faithful app, from the folder that holds `app.py` and `movies.csv`:

```bash
shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py
```

We can confirm the app is working by changing the x axis, y axis, and color dropdowns and watching the scatter plot update. Typing a title in the text box should leave the plot unchanged until we click Update plot title.

## Project structure

The movies app runs, but nothing in the folder tells another developer (or our future selves) which packages it needs or how the editor should be configured. The `02.3_proj-app` branch adds these files:

```bash
git checkout 02.3_proj-app
```

```default
pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
├── requirements.txt
└── utils.py
```

The app code (`app.py`, `utils.py`, and `movies.csv`) is unchanged. The branch adds `requirements.txt` and `.vscode/settings.json`, and it updates `README.md` and `.gitignore`.

### requirements.txt

`requirements.txt` lists the packages the app depends on, one per line:

```default
shiny>=1.2.0
matplotlib>=3.8.0
pandas>=2.1.0
numpy>=1.26.0
```

Each line sets a minimum version (`>=`), not an exact one. This makes `requirements.txt` a looser record than a lockfile: it guarantees a version that's new enough, but two people installing from it on different days can end up with different versions.[^shiny-requirements]

[^shiny-requirements]: `requirements.txt` fills a role similar to `renv.lock`, although `renv.lock` records exact versions and these entries are only lower bounds.

Anyone who clones the branch can create a virtual environment and install everything in `requirements.txt` with `-r`:

```bash
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If you're using Python's built-in `venv`, the equivalent install command is `pip install -r requirements.txt`. Once we turn the app into a package, the dependencies will move into `pyproject.toml` and the exact versions will be recorded in `uv.lock` (we saw both in the [Whole Game](whole_game.qmd) chapter, and the [Dependencies](dependencies.qmd) chapter covers them in detail).

### IDE settings

VS Code (and Positron, which is built on the same open source code base) reads project settings from `.vscode/settings.json`. The settings in this branch are below:

```json
{
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": ".venv/bin/python",
    "python.terminal.activateEnvironment": true,
    "editor.formatOnSave": true,
    "editor.rulers": [88],
    "[python]": {
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "ms-python.black-formatter"
    }
}
```

`python.defaultInterpreterPath` points the editor at the Python inside `.venv/`, and `python.terminal.activateEnvironment` activates the virtual environment whenever we open a new terminal. The remaining settings format Python files with [Black](https://black.readthedocs.io/) every time we save, and draw a ruler at 88 characters (Black's default line length). The Black formatter setting requires the [Black Formatter extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.black-formatter).

::: {.callout-note title="Sharing editor settings"}

The `.gitignore` in the earlier branches listed `.vscode/`, so editor settings were never committed. The `02.3_proj-app` branch removes that entry, which means `.vscode/settings.json` is shared with anyone who clones the repository.

:::

## Recap

In this chapter we built the app we'll use throughout the rest of the book, one branch at a time:

1. `02.1_shiny-app`: the Old Faithful app introduced the Core API, with a UI object built from `ui` functions, a `server()` function with `@render` outputs, and `App()` to combine them.
2. `02.2_movies-app`: the movies app added dropdown, text, and button inputs, read data from `movies.csv`, moved the plotting code into `scatter_plot()` in `utils.py`, and used `@reactive.calc` and `@reactive.event()` to control when the title updates.
3. `02.3_proj-app`: the project gained a `requirements.txt` for its dependencies and a `.vscode/settings.json` for its editor configuration.

The project is still a folder of loose files, though. The data path depends on the working directory, `utils.py` is only importable from the same folder, and `requirements.txt` doesn't pin exact versions. In the [Packages](packages.qmd) chapter we'll start turning this project into an installable Python package.
